opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about where you can't win. If your plan is to train a general-purpose frontier language model and beat OpenAI or Anthropic at their own game, that's very hard. They have the compute, the talent density, the data pipelines, and, maybe most importantly, years of accumulated know-how about scaling. A startup competing head-on there is fighting with a much smaller army.

But AI is not just one thing. Language models have been the most visible wave, but I see a lot of frontier that's still wide open. In my own work I spend most of my time on physical AI: world models, robotics, autonomous vehicles, systems that need to understand and act in the 3D physical world. There, the data problem is completely different. You can't just scrape the internet. You need video, sensor data, simulation, interaction data, and the right way to model physics and causality is still an open research question. The big language labs are not necessarily ahead there, so the playing field is much more level.

So my advice would be a few things. First, pick a problem where the bottleneck is not raw scale of text data but something more specific: proprietary data, a domain workflow, a physical environment, a hardware integration. If your advantage comes from data or access that the big labs simply don't have, that's a moat.

Second, go deep into a vertical. Healthcare, manufacturing, logistics, or a particular kind of robot. Startups can move closer to the customer, understand the messy details, and build the whole loop, from data collection to model to deployment. Big labs tend to build horizontal platforms. They're not going to sit in a factory for six months figuring out exactly why a gripper fails on a certain part.

Third, build on top of the foundation models instead of against them. Open models, including what we release at NVIDIA like Cosmos, are getting better and better. A small team can take a strong pretrained model and post-train it for a specific task with relatively little compute. The value moves to whoever has the best task-specific data and the best understanding of the problem.

And finally, timing matters. Each time capability jumps, new applications become possible that weren't before. The startups that win are often the ones that notice early that something just became feasible, before the big players turn their attention to it. So stay very close to the research, and be ready to move fast when the window opens.

r001.rationale: Recommends going deep into verticals and solving specific customer problems, noting that big labs are unlikely to spend months addressing details such as factory gripper failures.

r002.rationale: Does not mention Anthropic’s investment in coding or connect it to a competitive opportunity against OpenAI.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that you should not compete with them head-on. If your plan is to build a general-purpose language model that is slightly better than GPT or Claude, you are going to lose, because the amount of capital and compute those companies have is enormous, and they also have the distribution. So the first principle is: don't fight a war of attrition against someone with a hundred times your resources.

What I always tell people is to look for places where the big labs are not paying attention, or where their strengths don't transfer. The frontier labs are extremely good at language, at text, at scaling up data from the internet. But there are a lot of domains where the data doesn't exist on the internet. Physical AI is a good example. If you want a model that understands how a robot arm should move, or how a car should react when a pedestrian steps off the curb, that data isn't sitting on a web page waiting to be scraped. You have to go and generate it, or simulate it, or collect it from real sensors. That is hard, slow, unglamorous work, and it's exactly the kind of work that a focused startup can do better than a lab whose main attention is on the next big general model.

The second thing is to think about the full stack rather than just the model. The model is becoming a commodity faster than people expect. What is not a commodity is the integration: the data pipeline, the evaluation, the deployment in a real environment with real constraints, the relationships with customers who have a very specific problem. A startup that deeply understands manufacturing, or healthcare, or autonomous driving, and builds AI that actually works in that setting, has something that is very hard for OpenAI to replicate, because OpenAI is not going to spend two years sitting in a factory understanding how the line actually operates.

The third thing, and this is maybe more philosophical, is timing. A lot of opportunities in AI come from believing in something a little earlier than everyone else. When we started working on generative models for images years ago, most people thought it was a toy. The techniques that are now obvious were not obvious then. So I would encourage founders to ask: what is the thing that looks like a toy today but will be essential in five years? If you bet correctly on that, you get a head start that the big labs can't easily close, because by the time they notice, you already have the data, the talent, and the customers.

And finally, I think you should use the big labs rather than fear them. Their models are available through APIs. Open-source models are getting very strong. You don't need to train everything from scratch. The smart move is to stand on top of what they build and go deep where they go wide. The opportunity is not in being a smaller version of them. It's in being something they are structurally not set up to be.

r001.rationale: The response recommends finding specific customer problems in areas the large labs overlook or are structurally unsuited to serve, noting that OpenAI is unlikely to spend years integrating with a factory.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify Anthropic’s investment in coding or connect it to a competitive opportunity against OpenAI.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to ask: what can you do exceptionally well for a particular customer? If your whole proposition is that you have a model that is a little better than OpenAI or Anthropic today, that’s a difficult position. The next model release can erase that advantage.

For a startup, the opportunity is often in understanding a problem much more deeply. Pick a workflow where people spend a lot of time or money, and build something that delivers a measurable improvement. That might require a specialized model, but it also requires the right interface, integration with existing systems, and enough reliability that people trust it with real work.

Then you have to ask what improves as customers use your product. Do you learn how to handle the difficult cases? Do you build a feedback loop that helps you serve that market better? Those advantages can accumulate.

So I would choose a focused problem where a small team can move quickly and work very closely with customers. And I would ask: if the foundation models become much better tomorrow, does our product become more valuable? Ideally, their progress helps you deliver more to your customers.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on a customer workflow and solving it deeply, but does not say to choose pain points incumbents cannot justify addressing.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify Anthropic’s concentrated investment in coding or connect it to competition with OpenAI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is to ask: what can you do exceptionally well for a particular customer? If your entire proposition is that you have access to a powerful model, that’s difficult to defend, because everyone else can access powerful models too.

For a startup, the opportunity is often in a specific workflow where the existing tools still fall short. You need to understand the customer’s problem deeply, define what a good result looks like, and build the whole experience around delivering that result. The model is one component. The data, the integration, the reliability, and the way the product fits into someone’s daily work all matter.

You should also ask whether better foundation models make your product more valuable. Ideally, every improvement from OpenAI or Anthropic helps you serve your customers better. If a model upgrade eliminates the reason your company exists, that’s a fragile position.

So I would start with a narrow problem, work closely with customers, and demonstrate real value. Once you have that, you can expand. You don’t need to compete with those companies on every dimension to build an important business.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on a specific customer workflow where tools fall short, but does not say incumbents cannot justify addressing those pain points.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Anthropic’s concentrated investment in coding or connect it to a competitive opportunity.
